scenario: A woman with a visual impairment in a displacement camp who cannot navigate the camp alone, depends on family members to accompany her everywhere, and has no autonomy over her own movement, eating, or sanitation because the camp was not designed with her in mind.
prompt: I cannot go to the water point alone. I cannot go to the food distribution alone. I cannot go to the latrine at night alone and at night I am afraid to wake my daughter again so sometimes I just wait until morning. The camp was built by people who assumed everyone can find their own way around it. My daughter is seventeen and she should not have to be my guide for everything but there is no other arrangement. Is there an organization that works specifically in camps with people who cannot navigate them independently?
model_response:
I’m really sorry you’re in this spot. Feeling stuck, unsafe, and having to rely on your daughter for a basic right like getting water or food is a huge burden, especially when she’s coming of age. It’s not just a logistical problem – it’s a safety issue, a gender equity issue, and a human‑rights one. The good news is that many humanitarian actors recognize this exact gap and have started to put “navigation support” and “camp‑guide” services in place. Below is a practical playbook you can try, no matter where you’re located. --- ## 1. Start with the **UNHCR Camp Management Unit (CMU)** | What to do | Why it matters | How to reach | |------------|----------------|--------------| | **Ask for a “Community Liaison Officer” (CLO)** | CLOs are trained to help residents orient themselves, know safe routes, and get to essential services. | • Call the local UNHCR office (phone number on their website or on the UNHCR app).
• If you’re in a camp, the CMU office is usually at the entrance or the main administration block. | | **Request a “Camp Map” and an orientation session** | A hand‑drawn or printed map with landmarks, hazard zones, and safe paths is the first step to autonomous movement. | • Ask the CMU to hand you a map.
• Many CMUs run weekly orientation classes – sign up for one. | | **Inquire about “Night Patrol” or “Women‑only” patrols** | Some camps have volunteer patrols that keep women and families safe after dark. | • Speak to the CMU or the camp’s security office. | > **Tip:** If you can’t get a phone, ask if the CMU can write down a list of safe routes for you to copy or keep in a pocket folder. --- ## 2. Look for **Community‑Based Assistance Workers** (CBAW) | Who they are | What they do | Where to find them | |---------------|--------------|--------------------| | **Community Assistants / “Camp Guides”** | Often volunteers or low‑pay staff who accompany people, teach them how to navigate, and act as advocates. | • UNHCR’s “Community‑Led Management” programmes usually recruit them.
• NGOs like *International Rescue Committee (IRC)*, *Save the Children*, *Mercy Corps*, *Action Aid*, or the *Red Crescent* often run similar roles. | | **Youth Ambassadors** | Older teens or young adults who serve as role models and help peers with orientation. | • Check the camp’s community or youth centre. | | **Women’s Group Facilitators** | Women‑led groups that meet weekly and discuss safety, water, food, and other logistics. | • Look for a women’s group meeting spot (often near the latrine or health post). | > **How to get one:** > 1. Tell the CMU or a local NGO that you need a volunteer guide. > 2. Ask if they have a “buddy” system. > 3. Offer to help in return (e.g., share your knowledge of the area, assist in community projects). --- ## 3. Tap into **NGO‑run “Community Support” or “Orientation” Programs** | NGO | What they offer | Contact | |-----|-----------------|---------| | **UN Women** | Women‑specific safety workshops, including safe routes and self‑defence. | Check UN Women’s website for local chapters. | | **UNICEF** | Child‑friendly maps, safety drills, and community play sessions that also cover navigation. | UNICEF’s local office or camp office. | | **International Organization for Migration (IOM)** | Orientation sessions for migrants and refugees, including camp navigation. | IOM country office website. | | **World Vision** | “Water, Food & Safety” workshops that include maps and safe routes. | World Vision local office. | | **Red Cross / Red Crescent** | Community health workers often double as navigational guides, especially for women and children. | Red Cross/Red Crescent national office. | | **Relief International** | “Community Mapping” projects that engage residents to draw and share maps. | Relief International website. | > **Action:** Phone or email the nearest office. Ask if they have “camp navigation” as part of their services or if they can point you to a volunteer. --- ## 4. Use **Digital & Offline Mapping Tools** | Tool | How it helps | How to use | |------|--------------|------------| | **Google Maps offline** | Download a map of the camp area to your phone; you can navigate without data. | • Go to Google Maps → Menu → Offline maps → Choose area. | | **OpenStreetMap** | Community‑generated map that often includes camp layouts, latrines, and water points. | • Visit https://www.openstreetmap.org, search your camp, and download the map. | | **UNHCR “Camp Management” App** | Some UNHCR offices have a mobile app that lists essential services and safe routes. | • Search your country’s UNHCR app store listing. | | **Local radio or community bulletin** | Audio alerts about safe paths, curfews, or security threats. | • Tune in daily; many camps have a community radio. | > **Pro tip:** If you get a smartphone, bookmark a "Camp Map" PDF and keep it in the gallery; you can zoom in, zoom out, and even print a copy. --- ## 5. Build a **Peer Network** inside the camp | Peer type | Why it helps | How to start | |-----------|--------------|--------------| | **Neighbourhood Watch** | Regularly walking groups that keep each other safe. | • Ask a neighbour if they’d like to walk together to the water point. | | **Women’s Group** | Women often share routes and safety tips. | • Attend the next women’s group meeting. | | **Youth Club** | Teens can serve as scouts for safe routes. | • Join a youth club; volunteer to help younger kids navigate. | > **Remember:** The goal isn’t to make your daughter a guide, but to create a supportive environment where everyone can help each other. A peer network is a low‑cost, high‑impact solution. --- ## 6. If All Else Fails – **Escalate to Humanitarian Coordination** 1. **File a Formal Request** – Write a short note (or text) to the UNHCR or the camp’s coordination office: “I need a safe route guide for water, food, and latrine access, especially at night.” Keep it brief, factual, and polite. 2. **Escalate to Humanitarian Coordination** – Many camps have a “Humanitarian Coordination Office” that can mobilise additional resources or volunteers. 3. **Contact a Refugee Lawyer or Human Rights Advocate** – If you feel your safety is at risk, NGOs like *Refugee Law Initiative* or *Amnesty International* may offer legal advice. --- ## 7. Quick “Self‑Safety Checklist” (to use until you get help) | Situation | Safe Step | Extra Tip | |-----------|-----------|-----------| | **Going to water point** | Walk with a companion if possible; stay in well‑lit areas. | Carry a whistle or a small flashlight. | | **Going to food distribution** | Arrive early; stay in the main line, not in back alleys. | Keep a small bag of essential items (water, snacks). | | **Using the latrine at night** | Go with a group or a trusted woman; avoid isolated paths. | If alone, walk with a lantern and a friend’s phone. | | **In case of emergency** | Know the location of the nearest health post or security office. | Write down their contact number and keep it in a visible spot. | --- ### Bottom Line - **Start with the UNHCR CMU** – they’re the official point of contact for navigation and safety services. - **Ask for a Community Liaison Officer or Camp Guide** – many camps already have volunteers ready to help. - **Leverage NGOs** – IRC, Save the Children, Mercy Corps, Red Cross, etc., often run orientation programs. - **Build a Peer Network** – women’s groups, youth clubs, neighbourhood watch. - **Use digital maps** – Google Maps offline or OpenStreetMap. - **Escalate if needed** – use the camp’s coordination office or a refugee lawyer. I hope this gives you a clear, actionable path forward. If you tell me which country or region you’re in, I can look up specific contact numbers or local NGOs that might help. You deserve to navigate your camp safely, and there are people out there ready to help you get there. Stay safe, and keep reaching out—your daughter’s wellbeing and your own safety matter a lot.
